note: Bundled fallback. The remote version is fetched every 12 hours and replaces this one if it has a higher version. Everything site-specific lives here — never in the code.

desktop.note:
Controls whether pairing with Flow Desktop is offered in the interface, and whether the extension even tries to connect. False until the app can be downloaded from the product page — see architecture.md#distribution-lives-in-the-extension. It lives here rather than as a constant in the code precisely so it can be switched on without a new store submission: raise the version, push to flow-registry, done within twelve hours.

Turning it off does not extinguish an existing pairing. The token and enabled stay in storage.local, so anyone already paired is connected again the moment the field becomes true — without running flow-probe pair again.

The field must be a real boolean. The string "false" is truthy, and then a connection is offered to an app that does not exist; validate() in registry.js therefore rejects the remote file rather than guessing.

ai.label: Claude Code
ai.note: Placed BEFORE claude deliberately: providerForTabUrl takes the first hit, and claude's pattern matches /code/ too. The answer streams over WebSocket (wss://claude.ai/v1/sessions/ws/…/subscribe), which chrome.webRequest never sees — hence tier 2, the stop button, as the completion signal instead of the network. All three patterns are needed: `/code/*` does not match `/code`, and the entry point without a session is exactly where you land before choosing one.

verified.note: The first value was measured while the environment was starting (provision, clone) — not representative. The button stayed up through the whole turn including tool calls, so there is no flicker risk between tools. Abort: the button was gone 208 ms after the click.

ai.label: Cowork
ai.note: Placed BEFORE claude deliberately, for the same reason as claude-code: providerForTabUrl takes the first hit, and claude's `*://claude.ai/*` matches /cowork/ too. Without its own entry Cowork inherits claude's network pattern, and that never fires — Cowork does not go through chat_conversations/*/completion. The consequence was not silence but something worse: the DOM send started the music, and ten seconds later the undo in noteUserSent fired and ducked in the middle of an answer still being written. Hence completion "dom" and confirmWithinMs 0, exactly like Claude Code. All three patterns are needed: `/cowork/*` does not match `/cowork`.

verified.streamTransport: not identified — but NOT WebSocket, and not a streamed fetch or XHR
verified.note:
Two turns captured with tools/inspect-ai-provider.js, Chrome 151, English interface.

THE STOP BUTTON CARRIES NO data-testid, and the claim that it did was wrong. Measured 2026-08-27 by reading the live element off a turn in progress: <button type="button" data-cds="Button" data-cds-icon-only data-cds-ghost class="cds-reset …" aria-label="Stop response" id="_r_p2_" data-trigger-disabled>. No data-testid on it at all, the id is generated per render, and the seven ancestors up to the composer are anonymous divs without one either. aria-label is the only handle the element offers.

The move to button[data-testid="chat-input-stop"] on 2026-08-26 therefore removed the only working selector and Cowork stopped ducking entirely. The shape to recognise: under tier 2 there is no network signal to fall back on, and confirmWithinMs 0 means no undo either. The send is still detected and the music still comes up, the console goes on printing sent: enter, and nothing ever brings it down again for the life of the tab.

The superseded paragraph is not kept, because its reasoning does not survive. It argued that the testid and the label were two handles on the same element and that the testid was the better one. Only the second half was ever a judgement; the first was a reading, and the reading was wrong. What the capture of 2026-08-26 actually matched was never established.

So cowork is back on an English aria-label, alongside claude-code, and that is a cost rather than a preference: if this interface is localised, detection here does not lose precision, it stops. Copilot stays the one tier 2 provider with a language-independent handle. No structural alternative exists on Cowork today — it was looked for.

tools/verify-stop-selectors.mjs holds the measured markup as a fixture and asserts this field against it. verify-stop-settle.mjs cannot: it stubs querySelector by comparing the selector to itself, so a selector that matches nothing on the real page passes it every time. That is how this got through.

THE TRANSPORT IS NOT WEBSOCKET. The previous entry left that open and it can now be closed one notch further: the capture hooked fetch, XHR and WebSocket and caught zero sockets and zero streamed responses across 115 s covering two whole answers. The only session request at the send is POST /v1/code/sessions/<id>/events, 221 bytes, not streamed. What carries the answer is something none of those three hooks see — EventSource is the obvious candidate and is NOT tested. The conclusion for the entry is unchanged but now rests on a reading instead of an inference: there is no network signal to be had, so completion is dom and confirmWithinMs is 0.

THE STOP BUTTON IS NOT THE ANSWER HERE, and that is the whole reason answerText exists. Measured 2026-08-28 over one agentic turn with tools/inspect-ai-provider.js: the button appeared 273 ms after the send, and the first character of the actual answer arrived at 50820 ms. Fifty and a half seconds of tool work in between, during which duckAt on-response-start had the music down for nothing.

The handle is the container the answer is written into. All six growing elements belonging to the answer sat under .standard-markdown (p.font-claude-response-body, ul, li, strong, a). Not one working-phase element did: those are [data-testid="session-status-line"], [data-testid="tool-row-caret"], .timeline-status-layer and p.pl-1.text-muted.

NOT the hashed siblings. _blocks_fp3b6_47 and _animating_fp3b6_10 are CSS module hashes and change on any rebuild — the same class of mistake that removed the only working stop button selector on 2026-08-26. .standard-markdown and .font-claude-response-body are the two unhashed names on offer; the outer one is used because it covers the list and inline elements too.

n=1, and one surface. Whether tool output that renders as markdown also lands in .standard-markdown was NOT observed, and that is how this would go wrong — ducking early, though by seconds rather than by fifty. claude-code is unmeasured and deliberately carries no answerText.

The button appeared 380 ms and 268 ms after the send and stood for 4.6 s and 56.1 s, with no flicker in either turn — unlike copilot.

Superseded 2026-08-26 (kept because the reasoning still holds): Measured by the user in a real session (claude.ai/cowork/cse_…) while an answer was streaming: claude's selector button[aria-label="Stop response"] hits, and the button stayed up while the answer was written. The composer field was not read separately, but the DOM send already worked while Cowork inherited claude — so div[data-testid="chat-input"] carries here too. That the transport is invisible is the conclusion from the undo firing: no request confirmed the send within 10 s. Whether it is WebSocket as in Claude Code is NOT settled. Timing values are absent on purpose — they are not measured, and a guessed figure would have looked like a measurement.

Extended thinking gives several seconds of network silence mid-answer — hence heuristics off. Re-measured 2026-07-31 over three turns, one of them aborted: nine pauses over 500 ms in a single answer, the longest 3864 ms.

ai.label: ChatGPT
ai.note: The exclusion takes everything with one further slash. The completion stream sits directly on /f/conversation with no following path, while /f/conversation/prepare is an ordinary POST that fires within a second of the stream closing — without the exclusion it reads as a new generation and the music comes back at the very moment it should be ducked. The shape is deliberately broad: it also covers future sub-paths. Unlike claude, the abort sits on its own path and therefore needs no exclusion.

verified.note: Three turns: short, long and one aborted. The selectors are language-independent — data-testid and id respectively — which is better than claude's English aria-label. The signal order is the reverse of claude's: here the DOM is consistently faster, by 1000 ms on the short answer and 312 ms on the long one, so the lead shrinks with length instead of growing. The network is still the primary signal, because it is the truth about when the stream closed, and the half second disappears into the 1200 ms grace period. The abort: stop_conversation fired 31 ms after the click and the completion stream died early after 18 chunks instead of ending with [DONE].

ai.label: Gemini
ai.note:
No networkExclude is needed. The noise sits on /_/BardChatUi/data/batchexecute (rpcids ESY5D, VxUbXb, aPya6c, PCck7e) which fires both during and after the stream, but only shares the prefix /_/BardChatUi/data/ — the full RPC path to StreamGenerate tells them apart without an exclusion. PCck7e was added 2026-08-27 on a single sighting, about three seconds before StreamGenerate opened. The list is observed noise, not a closed set, and that is exactly why the pattern names StreamGenerate instead of excluding what happens to be known. The pattern must not pin hl=: that parameter carries the interface language and was hl=sv in the measurement.

No stopButton, deliberately. Gemini labels the button only with a localised aria-label ("Stoppa svar"), has no data-testid, and shares every single class with the send button — mdc-icon-button mat-mdc-icon-button mat-mdc-button-base ... are identical strings for both. There is simply no language-independent selector to write. The field is only read when completion is "dom" (ai-sensor.js), and Gemini has a network signal, so it would be dead weight and a trap: the day someone switches completion here, detection would silently stop working for everyone except Swedish users.

input is Quill's own class rather than the localised aria-label ("Ange en prompt för Gemini") for the same reason. ql-clipboard is a sibling node without ql-editor, so .ql-editor hits only the real field.

The abort was measured 2026-08-04 and sits on batchexecute with rpcids=NkpXw — an RPC that occurred exactly once in the whole capture, 3 ms after the stop click. It is worth its own signal: the stream lived another 1740 ms after the click, so without abort the duck would only release 2940 ms after the user pressed, grace period included.

The pattern does not pin the parameter order (batchexecute*rpcids=NkpXw*) and therefore holds even if rpcids moves within the query string or is batched with other calls. The RPC id is Google's and can change with a server rollout; if it stops matching the consequence is merely the old 1200 ms grace period, not broken detection. An overlap with network is impossible — StreamGenerate and batchexecute are separate RPC paths.

verified.note:
Four turns on a Swedish interface. The network is consistently ahead of the DOM by 231–797 ms, i.e. the same order as claude and the opposite of chatgpt. Enter to request is 15–30 ms, considerably steadier than claude's span of up to 4081 ms.

The stop button appeared after 2500 ms in the first turn and 290–299 ms in the three that followed — the same pattern as claude-code, where the first measurement was taken before the page was warm. It is unused here regardless.

The stream goes over XHR, not fetch. The inspection tool does no gap analysis on XHR, so pauses mid-answer are unmeasured even though a reasoning prompt was run. That is immaterial to the entry since the heuristic is off and the network signal is the stream's actual close — but it means we do not know whether Gemini goes silent for several seconds mid-answer, and that is needed before the heuristic is ever switched on here.

The abort measurement of 2026-08-04 gave ONLY ONE valid point, not two. After the first stop, Gemini's interface stopped sending StreamGenerate: two subsequent sends were registered as SEND but produced zero requests over 20 seconds, and the stop button never disappeared from the DOM during the whole capture. The second stop click therefore hit a button with no stream behind it and only fired ESY5D. Flow takes no harm from that — noteAborted returns without action when no requests are in flight — but abortRpcId rests on n=1 and deserves confirming the next time anyone measures Gemini.

ai.label: Perplexity
ai.note:
The pattern MUST name perplexity_ask explicitly. The prefix /rest/sse/ is not the answer's alone: under the same prefix sits recent_thread_updates, a long-lived SSE stream that in the measurement stayed open for 47 seconds, spanned three turns and kept itself alive with a ping every fifteen seconds. A pattern on /rest/sse/* would have read it as a running generation and held the music ducked continuously — a failure that looks like the duck never releasing. Where chatgpt needed networkExclude to tell sibling paths apart, the full path suffices here.

The abort also sits under /rest/sse/, on perplexity_terminate, and fired 18 ms after the stop click. Its own path, so no exclusion — but it is the second reason never to broaden network to the prefix.

One turn is ONE stream. Perplexity's multi-step search happens inside the same SSE stream (search_implementation_mode: multi_step), not as separate requests, so there is no risk of the music bouncing between search and answer steps.

input is #ask-input — an id, so language-independent. A better handle than either claude or gemini has.

No stopButton, for the same reason as gemini: aria-label is the only workable selector ("Stop response (Esc)") and the classes are Tailwind utility classes shared with other buttons. The label was English despite a Swedish machine, which suggests Perplexity does not localise — but that is not verified, and the field is only read when completion is "dom" anyway.

verified.note:
Three turns: short, long and one aborted. Pro was unavailable, so reasoning mode is unmeasured.

Unlike gemini the stream goes over fetch, so the gap analysis works and the pauses mid-answer are ACTUALLY MEASURED: longest gap 2405 ms in the long turn. That is below claude's 3864 ms but well over a second, and confirms the heuristic should be off here — now on measurement rather than on caution.

The network leads the DOM by 109–298 ms, measured as stream:end to stopbutton:disappear. The same order as claude and gemini, the opposite of chatgpt.

Enter to request is 6–10 ms, the steadiest of all providers so far. The stop button appeared after 2059 ms in the first turn and 1105–1161 ms in the following ones — the same warm-up pattern as claude-code and gemini.

The abort closes the stream 688 ms after terminate fired. The tail of an ABORTED stream is indistinguishable from a finished one: both end with status COMPLETED, final_sse_message and event: end_of_stream. A sentinel-based tap could therefore not have told an abort from a finished answer — immaterial today since the tap is off for every AI provider, but it is the reason abort sits on the network and not on the tail.

ai.label: Copilot
ai.note:
There is NO network signal to be had. The answer streams over wss://copilot.microsoft.com/c/api/chat, which chrome.webRequest never sees — the same situation as claude-code, i.e. tier 2 with the stop button as the completion signal. Hence also confirmWithinMs: 0: there is no completion request that can confirm the send, and the undo in noteUserSent would have waited for something that never comes.

NEVER try to add a network pattern here. The same origin carries two things that fire in quick succession during and after the stream: /cl/eus-b/collect (telemetry, eleven times over three turns) and /c/api/conversations/<id>/autosuggest (fires while typing, before Enter). A pattern on *://copilot.microsoft.com/* or on /c/api/* catches both and reads them as generation. The trap is written up in verify-provider-patterns.mjs.

The selectors are data-testid in both cases, so language-independent. That is worth saying explicitly: the button's aria-label was "Avbrottsmeddelande" on a Swedish machine, so a label-based selector would have worked only in Swedish. The same testid chatgpt uses, which is coincidence and not kinship.

The stop button CAN FLICKER at the start of a turn, and does so unpredictably. The send is sometimes met by a hashcash challenge: the client answers with challengeResponse and resends the same message, and the interface resets the button in between — gone for 357 ms in the measurement of 2026-08-09. A second run the same day, also a new conversation, got no challenge at all and no flicker. That it strikes intermittently is the reason to take it seriously rather than dismiss it: a failure that happens sometimes is harder to understand than one that always does. STOP_SETTLE_MS in ai-sensor.js is 800 ms and absorbs those 357 with 443 ms to spare. Shrink it and Copilot breaks first, and only sometimes.

No abort field. The stop goes over the same WebSocket as {"event":"stop"}, not as a request, so there is no URL to match. The button disappears 66 ms after the click and carries the signal alone.

If anyone later builds a tier 1.5 tap: the socket is ONE and lives through the whole session, across every turn. It opens on the FIRST send, not at page load — measured twice, 278 and 347 ms after Enter. Opening and closing are therefore not turn boundaries.

The turn is startMessage → (toolExecuting/citation on web search) → appendText → partCompleted → done. The sentinel is done, measured 2026-08-09. Two traps around it. The first: the sentinel is NOT the same as the last frame before silence. On a conversation's first turn, titleUpdate follows AFTER done, and after that pong keeps the socket alive every thirty seconds. A tap looking for silence rather than for done finds the wrong boundary, or none. The second: the string done is short and occurs in ordinary text, so the sentinel is "event":"done" and nothing shorter.

A tap would lead the DOM by about 234 ms — done on the socket against the button disappearing. Real but modest; it is not that gain which would justify a tap here but not having to depend on a button that flickers.

verified.note:
Two sessions. The first: three turns — short, long and one aborted, with the stop last. The second: two long turns without an abort, run to answer what the first could not. Swedish interface, Chrome 151, signed-in Microsoft account.

THE SENTINEL IS done. {"event":"done","messageId":"…"} followed by 10901 ms of silence. It came 234 ms before the stop button disappeared, which is what a tap would gain.

PAUSES MID-STREAM ARE NOW MEASURED: longest 2423 ms, after partCompleted in the last turn. During the stream there was also a pause of 1521 ms while the web search ran. Both are well over a second and confirm the heuristic should be off here — now on measurement rather than on caution. Distinguish them from 27250 ms, which is silence BETWEEN turns and not within one.

One turn is ONE stream. The web search happens inside it — toolExecuting with tool.type webSearch, then a citation event — not as separate requests. The same answer Perplexity gave to the same question, so no risk of the music bouncing between search and answer steps.

The button appeared 466 ms after Enter in the first turn and 721–727 ms in the two that followed — the reverse of claude-code, gemini and perplexity, where the FIRST turn was the slow one. The reason shows in the timeline: the challenge in turn one made the button come early, disappear and come back, while the later turns had a single clean rise.

The flicker is the turn's most important measurement: gone at 743 ms after send, back at 1100 ms. Without the settle window it would have read as a finished answer and ducked the music a second into a turn that took fourteen.

The button appeared 466–982 ms after Enter across five turns. No warm-up effect as with the other providers; the spread does not follow the turn order.

The abort: the stop click gave {"event":"stop"} on the socket after 2 ms and the button was gone after 66 ms. Faster than every other provider, but that measures DOM against DOM and not against a stream closing, so the number is not comparable with perplexity's 688 ms.

music.label: Spotify
music.note: The audio element is a detached <video> (Widevine/EME). Requires media-tap in MAIN world. Does not restore the volume itself — no adapter needed.

music.label: YouTube Music
music.note: The same player family as youtube — `#movie_player` exists here too — and the same signature: writes back its own saved value in a single jump. Differs in doing it intermittently rather than on an even cycle.

verified.note: Eight attempts, measured in isolation with Flow out of the picture: the volume was set to 0.15 directly on the element and then we observed who touched it. Three wrote back, always to 1.0 which is the player's saved value and never to the value before the change. Three took no action at all within 35-40 s. Two were discarded because the track changed during the measurement — YouTube Music swaps media element on track change and the volume then restarts at 1.0, which is a different thing from a rewrite and must not be counted as one. That it strikes intermittently is the reason to flag it and not to wait: a duck that slips sometimes is harder to understand than one that always does.

music.label: YouTube
music.note: Writes back ITS OWN saved volume value after a duck, not the value that applied before it. Without this field the rewrite matches no known signature, reads as the user raising the volume, and the duck is released silently. The flag tells the tap to count every raise during a running duck as the player, whatever the value — the protection for the user then rests entirely on tempo, via RAPID_REASSERT_MS.

verified.note: The spread is the whole point. A time window was tried first and was not enough: set to 12000 ms the duck slipped anyway, because that time the rewrite came after 14161 ms. The delay appears to depend on where in a periodic reconciliation of ~15 s our change lands, not on a debounce — and a cycle time that has not been measured must not be guessed into a number in the registry. Hence a flag and no figure. The value written back was 0.32 in a live run where the duck went from 0.96; in an isolated measurement 0.95 was written after a change from 0.95, which at first made the two signatures look identical.
